idiom_name: one class per table over PreparedStatement/ResultSet
implementation_notes: JDBC is the substrate: a PreparedStatement is compiled once and executed with bound parameters, ResultSet rows are copied field by field into record classes, and every resource is AutoCloseable - so the gateway is one class per table, each method owning exactly one statement, with the Connection supplied by the caller so transaction boundaries stay outside. This is the form to choose when no framework may be assumed or when statements need statement-level control (fetch size, batching, vendor SQL); pair it with try-with-resources and an explicit commit/rollback in the caller.
pitfalls: A leaked ResultSet or PreparedStatement pins server-side cursors and its connection until finalization, which in a pool appears as starvation under load.
Parameter indices are 1-based and type-silent: setObject with the wrong SQL type is detected by the database at execution time, often only for some values.
Holding the Connection in a singleton gateway breaks transaction scoping and pool semantics; construct the gateway per unit of work.

variants.name: Spring JdbcTemplate + SimpleJdbcInsert
variants.idiom_name: JdbcTemplate query methods + SimpleJdbcInsert per table
variants.implementation_notes: Where Spring is already present, the gateway becomes a small repository-style class delegating to JdbcTemplate (query/queryForObject/update with automatic resource release and DataAccessException translation) plus SimpleJdbcInsert, which is literally a multi-threaded, reusable per-table insert gateway: it reads table metadata from the JDBC driver, needs only the table name and a Map of column values, and returns generated keys via executeAndReturnKey. Choose it to delete boilerplate; keep plain JDBC inside the same class for statements the templates obscure.
pitfalls: SimpleJdbcInsert's metadata processing fails at construction (not at the call site) when the driver cannot describe the table's columns; usingColumns()/withoutTableColumnMetaDataAccess() is the escape hatch.
Spring's @Transactional proxies only work on externally invoked beans - calling the gateway from the same class silently runs without a transaction.
JdbcTemplate hands back the raw driver exception hierarchy; DataAccessException subclasses must be handled where the failure semantics matter.
